answer_raw:
Tell them exactly what you need and frame it as a request, not a command.
**Clear boundaries**—for example, “I’m quitting, so I won’t smoke in the house. Please don’t remind me every hour; I’ll let you know when I’m done.” A clear request is more likely to be respected [2].

Ask for the right kind of help.
**1‑800‑QUIT‑NOW** is a free, confidential coaching line that you can share with the family; it offers tips you can discuss together [2].
A support group that includes both the quitter and family members can provide shared accountability. While the Smoking Cessation group on Drugs.com has 176 members and 31 questions, its structure is not described in detail as a family-inclusive program [7].

The **Family Check‑Up** program is evidence‑based but targets families with children aged 2‑17, so it isn’t suitable for an adult quit attempt [8]. Look instead for adult‑focused programs or local health‑center counseling.

Use a **no‑nagging approach** that focuses on positive communication and teamwork. Strategies that build family habits without nagging emphasize clear goals and shared celebration of small wins [5].

Cravings and withdrawal are normal, but most symptoms **fade within a week or two** if you stay committed, so frame the temporary difficulty as a hurdle that will pass [3]. When family members check in, redirect them to a scheduled daily update you provide, keeping the conversation predictable and reducing impulse prompts.

If nagging or offers of cigarettes persist, set a consequence: let the family know you’ll pause the conversation or seek outside support until they respect your boundaries. Avoid giving cigarettes as a “treat” or accepting them—this reinforces the habit.

Because the evidence lacks Brooklyn-specific programs, check with local health resources or a nearby quitline for the latest options. A quick phone call or a local search will fill that gap.

Finally, be aware that **nicotine patches are not proven to be effective for quitting smoking** according to the study cited [4]. If you choose a nicotine replacement, discuss it with a clinician or a quitline counselor.
